title: Dig up the root (338–343)
hook: a tree cut down grows again if the root is sound; so suffering returns while craving lives

segments.voice: Yesterday, tanha, thirst, and your line: the creeper grows. Did you catch a craving while it was still a thread? Day two hundred nineteen.

Anyone who has cut down a stubborn bush knows what happens next spring. The stump sits there, looking finished, and then little green shoots come up all around it. You cut them, and they come back. The trunk was never the problem. The roots were still alive under the ground, patient and well fed. It's the same with a habit you thought you'd beaten, a temper you thought you'd outgrown, a worry you thought was gone. Yesterday the creeper. Today, what's underneath it. Today: dig up the root.
screen: `THE STUMP LOOKS FINISHED.` → `SHOOTS COME BACK IN SPRING.` → `THE ROOTS WERE STILL ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred thirty-eight puts it plainly. A tree that's been cut down will grow again, as long as its root is unharmed. In the same way, as long as the craving underneath hasn't been uprooted, suffering keeps coming back, again and again. The verse right before it gave a farmer's picture to go with it. In India, people dig up a tough grass called birana to get at its root, which is fragrant and valuable. We know that root today as vetiver, used in perfumes and cooling mats. So digging up the root isn't only destruction. You dig because what's underneath matters. Then the verses map the roots. They speak of thirty-six streams of craving, all running toward pleasure, and of channels running everywhere, with the creeper sprouting up wherever they reach. When you see the creeper springing up, the text says, cut its root with wisdom. Next comes a picture you can almost see: people driven by thirst run about like a snared hare, held in fetters, suffering again and again. Here's the quiet surprise in these verses. The root isn't the thing you crave. It isn't the phone or the snack or the praise. The root is the craving itself, and the not-seeing that feeds it. That's why the text says to cut it with wisdom, not with force. Chopping the trunk is willpower, and it's useful. Digging the root is understanding why, and that's what stops the shoots in spring.
screen: `CUT DOWN, IT GROWS AGAIN.` · `BIRANA GRASS, FRAGRANT ROOT.` · `THIRTY-SIX STREAMS, THE HARE IN THE SNARE.` · `CUT THE ROOT WITH WISDOM.` · then, large: `DIG THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one craving that keeps coming back for you, the one that sprouts again every spring. Now dig, gently, one layer at a time. What do I want, when I want this? And under that, what do I want? Maybe comfort, or rest, or to feel less alone. Don't force an answer. Just keep asking, softly, and notice whatever comes up. Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dig up the root. A cut tree grows again while its root lives: cut craving at the root, with wisdom, not force.
Your line: dig the root. Today, when your recurring craving sprouts, ask once, what am I really wanting? Day two hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In Buddhist teaching, craving is uprooted by insight rather than willpower alone; meditators investigate what lies beneath a recurring desire, and teachers often use the verse of the tree that grows back.

fork.reveal: a tree cut down grows again while its root is sound; the verses say to cut the root with wisdom, which means understanding the craving.

original.note: Pali mūla: root; verse 338 speaks of a tree whose root is unharmed.

trapdoor: what you thought: dig up the root means try harder to stop.
what it means: see the craving underneath the habit, and cut it with wisdom rather than force.
what a scholar hears: verse 337's birana grass is dug for its root, usira (vetiver); the 'thirty-six streams' of 339 are explained by the commentary as craving multiplied across the senses.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hare-in-the-snare paraphrase corrected to the text (342: held in fetters, suffering again and again; the 'tighter the more they struggle' detail is not in the verse); fork no longer repeats day 211's late-night snack.
Verse 338 is paraphrased (Müller: a tree cut down 'is firm so long as its root is safe, and grows again'); a Keeper may choose to quote it after checking SBE 10.
Birana grass and its root usira identified with vetiver (khus); confirm.
Thirty-six streams (339): commentary counts 3 kinds of craving across 6 internal and 6 external sense bases = 36; confirm.
